summary: Explains how to use authenticated encryption algorithms with the Encrypted Payload of IKEv2. These algorithms combine confidentiality and integrity in one operation. The document describes how IKEv2 messages are protected with them and gives details for using such algorithms, and it updates the IKEv2 specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally you lock a box and then seal it with tape in two steps. These algorithms do both in one go. This explains how a secure-tunnel setup can use that faster, simpler way.

questions: how does aes gcm work with ikev2
does ikev2 need a separate integrity algorithm with gcm
subtitle: How IKEv2 can protect its messages with one combined encrypt-and-authenticate algorithm such as AES GCM or AES CCM.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 protected its Encrypted Payload with a block cipher plus a separate integrity algorithm. Authenticated encryption algorithms do both jobs in one operation, and IKEv2 had no defined way to use them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an Encrypted Payload layout with an Initialization Vector and a single Ciphertext field that carries the integrity check, says what goes into the associated data and the nonce, and specifies AES GCM and AES CCM for it.
tldr.outcome: IKEv2 can negotiate AES GCM and AES CCM as the encryption transform with no separate integrity algorithm. The RFC updates RFC 4306 and has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

today: RFC 5282 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4306. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Combine Encryption and Integrity
sections.content:
An authenticated encryption algorithm combines encryption and integrity into a single operation. It turns plaintext into ciphertext that includes an integrity check. An AEAD algorithm (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) also protects extra data that is sent unencrypted.

IKEv1 could not use these algorithms, because encryption was separated from integrity verification, which was handled by a separate Hash or Signature Payload. IKEv2 (RFC 4306) uses an Encrypted Payload based on the design of ESP, which associates encryption and integrity in a way that makes AEAD algorithms usable. This RFC describes how, and specifies two algorithms: AES in Galois/Counter Mode (AES GCM) and AES in Counter with CBC-MAC Mode (AES CCM).
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of locking a box and then taping it shut as two jobs, one tool does both at once. This RFC shows how a secure-tunnel setup can use that tool.

sections.title: The Encrypted Payload Layout
sections.content:
This RFC updates Section 3.14 of RFC 4306. With an authenticated encryption algorithm, the Encrypted Payload is the payload header fields, then an Initialization Vector (IV) field, then a Ciphertext field that already includes the integrity check. Because of that, there is no separate Integrity Check Value field.

The Next Payload, C bit and Payload Length fields are unchanged. The plaintext that gets encrypted is the IKE payloads followed by Padding and a Pad Length. Padding may hold any value the sender picks, has no alignment requirement, and a recipient MUST accept any amount of it up to 255 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The sealed envelope has a label, a one-time number, and the scrambled message with its tamper check built in. No separate stamp is needed.

sections.title: IV, Nonce and Associated Data
sections.content:
For AES GCM and AES CCM the IV MUST be eight octets, and the encryptor MUST choose it so the same value is used only once for a given key. Counters and LFSRs are named as common ways to do this.

The default nonce is the salt followed by the IV. The salt comes from the shared keying material and is not sent in the payload. AES GCM MUST use this format with a 12-octet nonce, and AES CCM MUST use it with an 11-octet nonce, matching how they are used with ESP.

The associated data runs from the first octet of the Fixed IKE Header through the fourth octet of the Encrypted Payload, which is its payload header. It includes any payloads between them. The IV and Ciphertext MUST NOT be included. Together with the IV and plaintext checks, this covers the whole IKEv2 message, and the Encrypted Payload is always the last payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The outside of the envelope is checked but not hidden. The scrambled message inside is both hidden and checked.

sections.title: Keys, Salt and Identifiers
sections.content:
When AES GCM or AES CCM is used, the SK_ai and SK_ar integrity keys are not used and are treated as having size zero. Each SK_ei and SK_er encryption key also carries salt bytes. With a 128-bit AES key, a GCM key is 20 octets (a 16-octet cipher key plus 4 octets of salt) and a CCM key is 19 octets (16 plus 3).

The ENCR transform identifiers, already allocated by IANA, are: 14, 15 and 16 for AES CCM with 8-, 12- and 16-octet ICVs, and 18, 19 and 20 for AES GCM with 8-, 12- and 16-octet ICVs. A 16-octet ICV SHOULD be used, and 12-octet ICVs are NOT RECOMMENDED. The Key Length attribute MUST be given as 128, 192 or 256; 192 is NOT RECOMMENDED, and 256 SHOULD be used when more than 128 bits is appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side gets a secret key plus a little extra number to mix in. Short numbered labels tell both sides which recipe and key size they picked.

sections.title: Algorithm Selection and AEAD Names
sections.content:
RFC 4306 required both an encryption and an integrity algorithm for an IKE SA. This RFC updates that: when an authenticated encryption algorithm is chosen for any SA (IKE or ESP), an integrity algorithm MUST NOT be selected. If every encryption algorithm in a proposal is authenticated encryption, the proposal MUST NOT include integrity transforms.

The RFC also adds ten names to the AEAD_* framework of RFC 5116: four GCM variants with 8- and 12-octet tags (such as AEAD_AES_128_GCM_8) and six CCM variants with an 11-octet nonce (such as AEAD_AES_128_CCM_SHORT). A table maps each name to an ENCR identifier and key length. No 192-bit AEAD algorithms are defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the combined tool already checks for tampering, you must not add a second checker. The RFC also gives each recipe an official name.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC points to all of RFC 5116 for authenticated encryption security considerations, not only its security section. It says the considerations for AES GCM and AES CCM with ESP apply here, and that their use with IKEv2 creates no additional ones. For IKEv2 itself it refers to Section 5 of RFC 4306.

The ENCR identifiers were already assigned for ESP, so no IANA action is needed for them. IANA added ten entries to the AEAD Parameters Registry, numbered 5 through 14. Registration is not an endorsement of the algorithm or its security.
sections.plainLanguage: Using the combined lock for tunnel setup is no riskier than using it for the tunnel itself. Being on the official list does not mean it is a good choice.

items.title: Associated data
items.text: IKE header through the Encrypted Payload header. Integrity only.

items.title: IV
items.text: Eight octets, sent in the payload, never reused for a key.

items.title: Salt
items.text: From keying material, not sent. Joined with the IV to form the nonce.

items.title: Ciphertext
items.text: Encrypted payloads, padding and pad length, plus the integrity check.
